planting.note: Sow seed in fall so winter chilling breaks dormancy naturally, or set container transplants in fall or early spring into consistently moist to seasonally wet, acidic sandy soil typical of wet pine flatwoods and savanna edges in full sun.

directions: Chapman's aster, also called savannah aster, is restricted in the wild to seasonally wet, open pine savannas of the Apalachicola River basin in the Florida Panhandle and a small adjoining part of Alabama, where it is tracked as imperiled. It produces showy purple to blue-lavender ray flowers with pale yellow centers from August into November atop slender stems, giving strong late-season color where most prairie wildflowers have finished. Because it depends on periodically wet, fire-maintained savanna soils, it performs best in a sunny bog garden, rain garden, or low spot that stays consistently moist rather than a typical dry border. Its late nectar is valuable to bees and migrating butterflies, and growing it in cultivation helps take pressure off a genuinely rare wild population.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Species Profile
Atlas of Florida Plants, University of South Florida

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in average, well-drained to moisture-retentive soil in full sun to partial shade; Prince holds its dark foliage color best with several hours of direct sun.

directions: Prince is a selection of the native calico aster grown chiefly for its narrow, near-black purple-plum foliage, which holds its color on sturdy, well-branched stems all season rather than fading in summer heat like many dark-leaved perennials. In late summer and early fall the entire clump is smothered in tiny white, pink-centered daisies that stand out sharply against the dark leaves, a two-tone effect that reads as a specimen accent even from a distance. Unlike some spreading native asters it is a well-behaved clumper rather than an aggressive colonizer, making it easier to place in a mixed border. It draws late-season bees and small butterflies and, given the wide native range of the species into the Gulf South, tolerates regional heat and humidity better than most New England or New York aster cultivars.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall or spring in average to dry, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Eastern Star is a compact selection of the native white wood aster bred for dense flower coverage under trees.

directions: Eastern Star is a compact, heavy-flowering selection of the eastern woodland native white wood aster, distinguished by glossy near-black stems that set off its heart-shaped, toothed foliage. In late summer into fall it produces an unusually dense cover of small white, yellow-centered daisy flowers, ranking among top performers in shaded perennial trials for floral coverage and disease resistance. Unlike most garden asters it thrives in dry, partial-to-full shade under trees where few other native perennials bloom well, making it a valuable dry-shade companion for hostas, ferns, and heucheras. Its late nectar and pollen support woodland bees and other pollinators after most shade-garden bloom has finished for the season.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes
North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Arcturus develops its darkest stem and leaf color in full sun and lean, less fertile soil.

directions: Arcturus is an old heirloom selection of the native smooth aster, originally raised at the Royal Horticultural Society's Chiswick trial garden in the early twentieth century and later rediscovered and reintroduced from an Irish garden collection. Its glossy, near-black stems and dark-tinted foliage form a striking upright backdrop for the abundant lilac-mauve, yellow-centered daisy flowers that open in September and October. Like the straight species, it has powdery-blue foliage tones earlier in the season and shrugs off the summer humidity and foliar disease that trouble many garden asters. The late bloom is an important nectar source for migrating monarchs and native bees, and the dark stems keep the clump ornamental even before flowering begins.
